## What's this all about?

A whole text adventure can start with one good room. In this activity you'll build a single location as a Python dictionary, display it with a triple-quoted f-string, and then invite a classmate to imagine where one of the exits leads.

This is a warm-up for the Week 6 assignment. You do **not** need movement, inventory, a command loop, or a complete game here. One room.

## Start with one room dictionary

```{python}
room = {
    "title": "THE MIDNIGHT LAUNDROMAT",
    "description": """Every washing machine has stopped at exactly 11:57.
One dryer is still turning, although it is not plugged in.""",
    "exits": {"back": "alley", "down": "basement"},
    "item": "one warm red sock",
}
```

The dictionary names four kinds of information. The description uses three quotation marks so it can run across a line break.

## Turn the data into a room card

```{python}
exit_words = ", ".join(room["exits"].keys())

room_card = f"""
+----------------------------------------+
LOCATION: {room["title"]}
+----------------------------------------+
{room["description"]}

EXITS: {exit_words}
ITEM:  {room["item"]}
+----------------------------------------+
"""

print(room_card)
```

The labels matter more than the border. Someone should be able to understand the location, the exits, and the object even if the lines wrap differently on their screen, or they're hearing it read aloud.

## Make your room

Create your own dictionary and room card. Your room needs:

1. A short location key or title.
2. A description of two or three lines written as a triple-quoted string.
3. At least two exits stored as direction-to-destination pairs.
4. One object someone might collect, examine, or avoid.
5. A labeled display built with an f-string.

```{python}
# YOUR ROOM DICTIONARY AND DISPLAY GO HERE
```

Keep it safe to share and easy to read. Your room can be eerie, funny, ordinary, dreamy, historical, futuristic, whatever you like. I'm not grading your prose or your ASCII art.

## Reflection

Answer in a sentence or two each:

1. Which details are stored as data, and which parts of the display are supplied by your formatting code?
2. Which exit would you most want another student to continue, and what mood or clue should they preserve?
3. Could someone understand every important detail without relying on the border, spacing, or visual layout?

## What to post

Post to the Week 6 discussion:

2. Your room dictionary or notebook link.
3. Your three reflection answers.

Reply to two classmates. For each one, pick an exit and pitch the room on the other side in two or three sentences. Keep at least one detail from their room so the two places feel like the same world.
